rows.verified: Leptospirosis is a zoonotic bacterial infection caused by pathogenic Leptospira species.
Rodents, cattle, pigs and other mammals can carry Leptospira and spread the bacteria in urine.
People can become infected through direct contact with animal urine or urine-contaminated water and environments.
The bacteria can enter through broken or waterlogged skin and through the eyes, nose or mouth.
Heavy rainfall and flooding can increase exposure to urine-contaminated water.
Agricultural, veterinary, pest-control, construction and canal work are recognised occupational exposure settings.
Preventive measures include handwashing, promptly cleaning wounds, showering after exposure and covering cuts with waterproof dressings.
Avoiding rodent contact and using appropriate protective clothing can reduce infection risk.
Leptospirosis risk depends on animal reservoirs, water contamination, rainfall, skin condition, exposure route, duration and protective measures.
UKHSA leptospirosis evidence is exposure-, environment-, occupation-, organism- and person-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.
Hantaviruses are carried mainly by rodents such as rats, mice and voles.
People can become infected through exposure to infected rodent urine, faeces or other excreta.
Hantavirus illness can range from mild flu-like disease to severe respiratory or haemorrhagic disease with kidney involvement.
The distribution of individual hantaviruses is closely linked to the ecology of their small-mammal hosts.
A small number of UK cases without overseas travel have been associated predominantly with pet-rat exposure.
UKHSA assesses the overall risk to the general public from Seoul hantavirus as very low.
Forestry, farming, trapping and military work can involve increased occupational exposure to hantaviruses.
Contact with rodent excreta during wood-pile work or cleaning abandoned buildings is a recognised exposure route.
Hantavirus risk depends on virus and host species, geography, rodent activity, aerosol or contact exposure, cleaning method and individual factors.
UKHSA hantavirus evidence is virus-, host-, location-, exposure- and person-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.
